quiz.q: According to the chapter, science is best described as:
o: A list of facts to memorise
A process: a way of thinking that welcomes curiosity and asks questions
Something done only in big laboratories
quiz.why: The chapter says science is a process, a way of thinking that welcomes curiosity, asks questions and is open to the unknown.

quiz.q: The page numbers of the Curiosity Grade 7 book follow the flight of:
o: A butterfly and a paper plane
quiz.why: The page numbers follow the playful flight of a butterfly and the soaring of a paper plane.

quiz.q: Why does a haldi stain on a uniform turn red when washed with soap?
o: Soap is basic, and haldi turns red in basic substances
quiz.why: Haldi is a natural indicator that turns red in basic substances such as soap.

quiz.q: Which object, placed in a circuit tester, will make the lamp glow?
quiz.why: Iron is a metal; metals let electric current pass.

quiz.q: Which of these changes can be reversed?
quiz.why: Melted ice can be frozen back into ice; the others cannot be undone.

quiz.q: An ice cube is put in a glass of water. Heat flows:
o: from the ice to the water
from the water to the ice
quiz.why: Heat flows from a hotter object (water) to a colder one (ice).

quiz.q: What makes water evaporate from the seas in the water cycle?
quiz.why: The chapter says that with the heat from the Sun, water evaporates from the seas.

quiz.q: How did early humans tell the time before clocks?
o: By looking at the position of shadows in the Sun
quiz.why: Early humans observed the shadows of objects in the Sun and used their position to tell the time.

o: the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth
the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
the Sun goes behind a cloud
quiz.why: In a solar eclipse the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth and its shadow falls on the Earth.

quiz.q: We have day and night because:
o: the Sun switches off at night
the Moon blocks the Sun every evening
the Earth rotates on its axis
the Earth stops going around the Sun at night
quiz.why: As the Earth rotates, our side faces towards the Sun (day) and then away from it (night).

qs.q: The chapter says that 'to be a wise person, you must be a ___ person'.
qs.ans: (b) whys: asking 'why' questions is the heart of science.

qs.q: Which taste tells us that a fruit contains an acid?
qs.ans: (c) Sour: sour fruits such as lemon and tamarind contain acids.

qs.q: Which of these is a metal?
qs.ans: (a) Copper is a metal and conducts electricity.

qs.q: Which change cannot be reversed?
qs.ans: (c) A ripe mango cannot become raw again.

qs.q: Rainwater that trickles into the ground can:
o: flow underground and be found far away
qs.ans: (d) It becomes groundwater and can flow underground, far away.

qs.q: During a lunar eclipse, the body in the middle is the:
qs.ans: (b) Earth: the Moon moves into the Earth's shadow.

qs.q: Name two fields of science mentioned in the chapter and say what the chapter tells us about how they are related.
qs.ans: Any two of physics, chemistry, biology, earth sciences (1 mark). They are interconnected: ideas in one area inspire discoveries or questions in another (1 mark).

qs.q: What happens to a haldi stain when it is washed with soap? Why?
qs.ans: It turns red (1 mark), because soap is basic and haldi (an indicator) turns red in basic substances (1 mark).

qs.q: Give one example each of a change that can be reversed and one that cannot.
qs.ans: Can be reversed: ice melting into water (1 mark). Cannot be reversed: fruit ripening / battery running out / rock breaking into pebbles (1 mark).

qs.q: State two life processes that animals need in order to grow.
qs.ans: Any two: eating food (nutrition), breathing, circulation of blood carrying nutrients (1 + 1 marks).

qs.q: Explain how a stick's shadow can be used to tell the time of day.
qs.ans: The Sun's position in the sky changes during the day (1 mark). In the morning and evening the Sun is low, so the shadow is long; around noon the Sun is highest, so the shadow is shortest (1 mark). The shadow also changes direction (west in the morning, east in the evening), so its length and position tell the time (1 mark).

qs.q: Describe the journey of water in nature as given in the chapter.
qs.ans: The Sun's heat makes water evaporate from the seas (1 mark). The vapour forms clouds and falls as rain (1 mark). Some rain trickles into the ground and may flow underground, far away (1 mark).

sections.name: Section D — Long answer / case based

qs.q: Meera puts objects one by one in the gap of a circuit made of a cell, a switch, wires and a lamp: a copper wire, a plastic scale, an iron nail, a rubber eraser and an aluminium foil strip. (a) Which objects make the lamp glow? (b) What do they have in common? (c) Why does the lamp not glow with the others? (d) If the switch is off, will the copper wire make the lamp glow? Explain.
qs.ans: (a) Copper wire, iron nail, aluminium foil (1.5 marks). (b) They are all metals, which let electric current pass (1 mark). (c) Plastic and rubber do not let current pass, so the circuit is not complete (1 mark). (d) No: an open switch breaks the circuit, so no current flows (1.5 marks).

qs.q: 'Science is about discovery and also about responsibility.' Explain this statement with the help of an example from your surroundings.
qs.ans: Discovery: science helps us understand how things work through questions and experiments (1 mark). Responsibility: human activities are linked to the natural world and society (1 mark). Example: plastic and waste thrown into a river pollute the water and harm fish (1 mark). Science can test the water and find solutions such as separating waste, composting flowers, using cloth bags (1 mark). This helps create a more sustainable world (1 mark).

qs.q: Which of these is a 'deeper question' of the kind the chapter wants us to ask?
o: What is the name of my school?
How many pages are in this book?
What colour is the sky today?
qs.ans: (b) The chapter lists: How do things work? Why do events happen? What can we learn from patterns?

qs.q: Lemon juice is sour because it contains:
qs.ans: (a) Lemon contains citric acid.

qs.q: Heat flows from:
o: a colder object to a hotter object
a hotter object to a colder object
qs.ans: (b) Heat always flows from hotter to colder.

qs.q: Plants make their food mainly in their:
qs.ans: (d) Green leaves make food using sunlight, water and carbon dioxide.

qs.q: A shadow forms when:
o: there is no light at all
qs.ans: (a) An object blocking light produces a shadow.

qs.q: The Earth's rotation on its axis causes:
qs.ans: (c) Day and night: the side facing the Sun has day.

qs.q: Why did the chapter mention the paper plane? What does it teach about science?
qs.ans: A simple paper plane inspired real scientific explorations of flight (1 mark). It shows that science begins with simple observations and experiments (1 mark).

qs.q: Haldi paper stays yellow in both lemon juice and water. Can we say both are the same type of liquid? Explain.
qs.ans: No (1 mark). Haldi changes colour only in basic substances; lemon juice is acidic and water is neutral, so another test is needed to tell them apart (1 mark).

qs.q: Do plants breathe? How?
qs.ans: Yes, plants breathe all the time, taking in oxygen and giving out carbon dioxide (1 mark). Air goes in and out through tiny pores (stomata) in the leaves (1 mark).

qs.q: What is a solar eclipse? On which day can it occur?
qs.ans: When the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth and its shadow falls on the Earth (1 mark). It can occur only on a New Moon day (1 mark).

qs.q: Batteries run out, ice melts, fruits ripen and rocks break into pebbles. Classify these changes as reversible or irreversible, giving a reason for any one.
qs.ans: Reversible: ice melting (1 mark). Irreversible: battery running out, fruit ripening, rock breaking into pebbles (1 mark). Reason: melted water can be frozen back to ice, but a ripe fruit can never become raw again (1 mark).

qs.q: Why does the chapter say we must 'step out of this book' to learn science?
qs.ans: Science is learnt through activities and experiments, not only reading (1 mark). These experiences are stepping stones to a deeper understanding of our environment and our place on the planet (1 mark). They help us see science as an ongoing process of discovery (1 mark).

sections.name: Section D — Long answer / case based

qs.q: Arjun ties a stone to a string to make a pendulum of length 1 m. It takes 2 seconds for one oscillation. (a) What is one oscillation? (b) How many oscillations will it make in one minute? (c) Farhan replaces the stone with a heavier one on the same string. What happens to the time? (d) What should they change to make it swing faster? (e) Why are pendulums useful for measuring time?
qs.ans: (a) Moving from one end to the other and back again (1 mark). (b) 60 ÷ 2 = 30 oscillations (1 mark). (c) The time stays the same; mass does not affect it (1 mark). (d) Make the string shorter (1 mark). (e) Each oscillation takes the same time, so the regular swing can be counted to measure time (1 mark).

qs.q: Draw a labelled diagram showing the positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon during (a) a solar eclipse and (b) a lunar eclipse. Explain each.
qs.ans: (a) Sun — Moon — Earth in a line; the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth (diagram 1 mark, explanation 1.5 marks). (b) Sun — Earth — Moon in a line; the Moon enters the Earth's shadow (diagram 1 mark, explanation 1.5 marks).

qs.q: Which of these is NOT one of the fields of science listed in the chapter?
qs.ans: (d) Astrology is not a science; the chapter lists physics, chemistry, biology and earth sciences.

qs.q: Haldi is called a natural indicator because it:
qs.ans: (b) It changes colour (to red) in basic substances.

qs.q: A torch battery that has run out:
o: can be used again after freezing
qs.ans: (b) The chapter says a torch battery runs out and can't be used again.

qs.q: Which carries nutrients from food all over our body?
qs.ans: (a) Blood circulates nutrients all over the body.

qs.q: Around noon, a stick's shadow is:
qs.ans: (c) The Sun is highest around noon, so the shadow is shortest.

qs.q: Which statement about eclipses is correct?
o: Only the Moon can cast a shadow
Both the Earth and the Moon can cast shadows, causing eclipses
qs.ans: (d) The chapter says even the Earth and Moon cast shadows, leading to eclipses.

qs.q: Give two examples from the chapter showing that science covers things 'small and large, near and far'.
qs.ans: Small: tiny cells inside a leaf (1 mark). Large/far: movement of the Sun and stars, or water flowing underground (1 mark).

qs.q: What kind of materials do we need to make a lamp glow in a circuit? Give two examples.
qs.ans: Materials that let current pass, mostly metals (1 mark). Examples: copper wire, iron nail, aluminium foil (any two, 1 mark).

qs.q: Why does an ice cube placed in a glass of water melt?
qs.ans: The water is warmer than the ice (1 mark). Heat flows from the warmer water to the colder ice, so the ice melts (1 mark).

qs.q: Why do our bodies change rapidly in the middle-school years? What do we need for this growth?
qs.ans: We are growing quickly at this age (1 mark). We need life processes: eating food, breathing, blood circulating nutrients (1 mark).

qs.q: Explain with an example how an experiment that confirms our idea can still lead to new questions.
qs.ans: Example: we test pendulums of the same length with different masses and find the time is the same, which confirms our idea (1 mark). New question: does the size of the swing change the time? (1 mark). This needs another experiment, so science keeps evolving (1 mark).

qs.q: How do green plants get their food? Name the things they need.
qs.ans: They make their own food (1 mark) in green leaves (1 mark) using sunlight, water and carbon dioxide from the air (1 mark).

sections.name: Section D — Long answer / case based

qs.q: Activity 1.1 'Question the Answer': (a) What is the aim of this activity? (b) Write two different questions for the answer 'Just make it half!'. (c) Write one creative question for the answer '42' that is not 'What is 32 + 10?'. (d) Why does the book say there are never any wrong questions?
qs.ans: (a) To think like a scientist by asking interesting questions, not just answering them (1 mark). (b) e.g. 'How do we get equal shares of cake?'; 'My essay is too long' (2 marks). (c) e.g. 'How many legs do 7 insects have altogether?' (7 × 6 = 42) (1 mark). (d) To encourage imagination and curiosity; asking freely leads to new ideas (1 mark).

qs.q: Describe the role of the Sun in (a) the water cycle, (b) telling time with shadows, (c) day and night.
qs.ans: (a) Its heat makes water evaporate from seas; vapour forms clouds and rain (2 marks). (b) As its position changes, shadows change length and direction, which tells the time (1.5 marks). (c) The Earth rotates; the side facing the Sun has day, the other side night (1.5 marks).

qs.q: Early inventors interested in flight studied:
qs.ans: (b) Early inventors studied bird wings.

qs.q: Tamarind tastes sour because it contains:
qs.ans: (a) Tamarind contains tartaric acid.

qs.q: Which pair of objects will both stop a lamp from glowing in a tester?
qs.ans: (d) Plastic and wood do not let current pass.

qs.q: Which change happens faster when heated?
o: The Moon going around the Earth
qs.ans: (a) Heating makes ice melt faster.

qs.q: The Moon goes around the:
qs.ans: (b) The Moon goes around the Earth, and the Earth around the Sun.

qs.q: A pendulum's time of oscillation depends on its:
qs.ans: (c) Length: the mass does not change it.

qs.q: What is meant by saying 'science is ever-evolving'?
qs.ans: Science keeps changing and growing (1 mark) because experiments lead to new questions, which need more experiments (1 mark).

qs.q: Name one acidic and one basic substance found at home.
qs.ans: Acidic: lemon juice / vinegar / tamarind (1 mark). Basic: soap solution / baking soda solution (1 mark).

qs.q: At 9 a.m. the Sun is in the east. In which direction will a pole's shadow point? Why?
qs.ans: Towards the west (1 mark), because a shadow forms on the side opposite to the light source (1 mark).

qs.q: Why don't we see an eclipse every month?
qs.ans: The Moon's path around the Earth is slightly tilted (1 mark), so the Sun, Earth and Moon line up exactly only sometimes (1 mark).

qs.q: How are human activities linked to the natural world? Give two examples and one way science helps.
qs.ans: Example 1: cutting trees reduces homes for birds and animals (1 mark). Example 2: throwing waste into rivers pollutes the water (1 mark). Science helps by studying the problem and finding sustainable solutions, e.g. planting trees, treating waste water (1 mark).

qs.q: Explain why the Earth has day and night with the help of a simple activity using a torch and a ball.
qs.ans: Shine a torch (Sun) on a ball (Earth) in a dark room (1 mark). Only the half facing the torch is lit: day; the other half is dark: night (1 mark). Turning the ball slowly (rotation on its axis) brings each place into light and then darkness: day and night (1 mark).

sections.name: Section D — Long answer / case based

qs.q: Gurpreet tests five liquids with haldi paper: water, lemon juice, soap solution, vinegar, baking soda solution. (a) In which liquids does the paper turn red? (b) In which does it stay yellow? (c) What does the red colour tell us? (d) Why does a haldi-stained shirt turn red when washed with soap?
qs.ans: (a) Soap solution and baking soda solution (1.5 marks). (b) Water, lemon juice, vinegar (1.5 marks). (c) The liquid is basic (1 mark). (d) Soap is basic, so the haldi in the stain turns red (1 mark).

qs.q: The chapter says that plants and animals both need life processes. Compare plants and animals for (a) getting food and (b) breathing. Why does the chapter call this 'beautiful and carefully balanced'?
qs.ans: (a) Animals eat food; plants make their own food in leaves using sunlight, water and carbon dioxide (2 marks). (b) Both breathe: animals through lungs/other organs, plants through tiny pores (stomata) in leaves (2 marks). Over time life has evolved so that these processes work together and keep living things alive in balance (1 mark).

qs.q: According to the chapter, great scientists:
o: ask amazing questions as well as answering them
qs.ans: (c) Great scientists don't just answer questions, they ask amazing ones.

qs.q: Which of these will conduct electricity even though it is a non-metal?
qs.ans: (b) Graphite is a non-metal that conducts electricity.

qs.q: Glaciers melt because:
o: heat flows into the ice from warmer surroundings
they are pulled by the Moon
cold flows out of them into the Sun
qs.ans: (a) Heat flows from the warmer surroundings into the colder ice.

qs.q: In the water cycle, clouds are formed from:
qs.ans: (c) Water vapour rises, cools and forms clouds.

qs.q: The evening shadow of a pole points towards the:
qs.ans: (d) In the evening the Sun is in the west, so the shadow points east.

qs.q: During a solar eclipse, the order of the three bodies is:
qs.ans: (a) The Moon is between the Sun and the Earth.

qs.q: Write any two questions about materials that the chapter says we will explore this year.
qs.ans: Why are some fruits sour? (1 mark) What happens when we wash a haldi stain on our school uniform? / What materials make a lamp glow? (1 mark)

qs.q: Why is it said that 'experiments are stepping stones'?
qs.ans: Each experiment builds understanding step by step (1 mark), leading to a deeper understanding of our environment and our place on the planet (1 mark).

qs.q: A pendulum makes 30 oscillations in one minute. How long does one oscillation take?
qs.ans: 60 s ÷ 30 = 2 s (working 1 mark, answer 1 mark).

qs.q: Name the two movements of the Earth mentioned in the chapter.
qs.ans: Rotation of the Earth around its axis (1 mark); the Earth going around the Sun (1 mark).

qs.q: Give a creative question for each answer: (a) 'Just add some milk.' (b) 'Don't panic, I have my towel.' (c) 'Because the cat's teeth were crooked.'
qs.ans: Any creative, sensible question for each (1 mark each). e.g. (a) 'My chai is too strong. What should I do?' (b) 'A boat splashed water all over us!' (c) 'Why did the bite marks on the mango look so strange?'

qs.q: How is light useful to us? Mention three ways given or suggested in the chapter.
qs.ans: Light helps us see (1 mark). Artificial light lets us read at night (1 mark). Shadows formed by light help tell time, and studying light has given a deep understanding of the universe (1 mark).

sections.name: Section D — Long answer / case based

qs.q: The chapter gives a 'quick journey' through the book. List any five topics you will study this year and write one question you would like to ask about each.
qs.ans: Any five topics with a sensible question (1 mark each), e.g. Acids and bases: why is curd sour? Electricity: why do wires have plastic covers? Changes: why does iron rust? Heat: why do steel spoons get hot in tea? Water: where does a well get its water? Life processes: how does blood move? Time: how does a pendulum clock work? Light: why are shadows longer in the evening? Earth and Moon: why does the Moon change shape?

qs.q: Farhan wants to find out whether the mass of the bob changes the time of a pendulum's oscillation. (a) What should he change? (b) What should he keep the same? (c) How should he measure the time accurately? (d) What result will he find? (e) What new question might he ask next?
qs.ans: (a) Only the mass of the bob (1 mark). (b) Length of string and how far he pulls it (1 mark). (c) Time 10 or 20 oscillations with a watch and divide by the number (1 mark). (d) The time stays the same; mass does not matter (1 mark). (e) e.g. 'Does the length change the time?' or 'Does the size of the swing matter?' (1 mark).
